title: Isolated Slabless Reshuffle (ISR) Blueprint
content:
Summary:

This note proposes the Isolated Slabless Reshuffle (ISR) allocator: a memory-layout and eviction architecture designed to reduce fragmentation and tail latency for multi-tenant KV caches without using traditional fixed-size slabs. ISR targets workloads with wide variance in sequence lengths and transient hot prefixes, where slabting causes internal waste and slabless designs suffer fragmentation over time.

Motivation / Problem statement:
- Slab allocators reduce fragmentation for uniform object sizes but waste memory when token sequences vary.
- Pure slabless arenas minimize internal waste but develop external fragmentation and slow background compaction, causing unpredictable latency spikes during reshuffle windows.
- Tenants with bursty prefixes create hot lanes that should be isolated (to avoid noisy neighbors) but still benefit from global reuse when idle.

Goals:
1) Keep steady-state allocation/eviction fast (O(1) common path) for reads/writes at tail latency targets.
2) Bound fragmentation so that background maintenance can be incremental and non-disruptive.
3) Provide isolation primitives so tenant/route hotness doesn't force global compaction.
4) Enable graceful, tunable tradeoffs between memory efficiency and CPU spent on reshuffle work.

Key concepts / terminology:
- microsegment: a contiguous allocation unit (e.g., 4KB or 16KB) which can contain multiple variable-length entries.
- lane: logical hotness group (tenant/route/prefix) with its own admission counters and soft quota.
- lane fence: a lightweight isolation marker that prevents immediate cross-lane compaction of slots until certain thresholds are met.
- reshuffle: incremental relocation of live entries to reduce fragmentation and coalesce free microsegments.
- drift compaction: background, low-priority pass that tolerates short-lived reclaims which are cheaper than immediate eviction.
- proactive stitcher: a small cooperative thread that stitches adjacent free microsegments when it detects long contiguous run of free segments.

Design overview:
ISR composes three layers: allocation front-end, retention/eviction policy, and background reshuffle/compaction.

1) Allocation front-end (fast path):
- Requests allocate from a per-core fast-bucket (cache of microsegments) that is previously warmed. Each microsegment in the fast-bucket has a small allocation bitmap and a microsegment header containing owner lane id, timestamp, and a small generation counter.
- Allocations within a microsegment are variable-length and use bump pointer + per-segment freelist for recycled slots. Common-case allocate is bump-only and never touches global locks.

2) Retention & eviction policy (policy path):
- Admission is lane-aware: each lane maintains an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) of recent byte-traffic and an admission throttle.
- When global memory pressure crosses a threshold, eviction victims are selected by lane-priority sampling: sample N microsegments across lanes with probability proportional to lane pressure (pressure = recent bytes - soft quota). Within a microsegment choose least-recently-used candidate via per-segment access counters.
- Eviction does not immediately free microsegments; instead, entries selected for eviction are marked tombstone and given a short grace TTL to allow a quick resurrect (common with hot tail replays). Immediate tombstone-free microsegments are enqueued for reshuffle scheduling.

3) Background reshuffle and fragmentation mitigation (maintenance path):
- The reshuffle subsystem runs as multiple cooperative workers with three prioritized queues: lane-local reshuffle (highest), cross-lane stitch (medium), and global drift compaction (low).
- Lane-local reshuffle tries to compact a lane's microsegments by moving live entries into least-fragmented microsegments that are owned by the same lane, honoring lane fences to avoid cross-tenant moves under high load.
- Cross-lane stitch opportunistically coalesces free microsegments from low-pressure lanes into larger free runs and yields them back to global pools.
- Drift compaction performs probabilistic picking of aged microsegments for deeper compaction and use a small budgeted I/O/CPU slice per worker to bound tail latency impact.

Memory layout specifics:
- Microsegment size is a tunable knob; default proposal = 16KB for GPU-hosted DRAM; smaller (4KB) may be used for latency-sensitive CPU-only hosts.
- Microsegment header fields (compact): owner_lane (16 bits), epoch (16 bits), allocation_bitmap_offset (16 bits), free_bytes_hint (16 bits), access_clock (32 bits). Small header ensures metadata is cache-friendly.
- Free runs are tracked using a shadow free-map per NUMA node to allow lock-free approximate search for contiguous microsegments. The shadow map is eventually consistent; the authoritative free-map is updated by stitch workers.

Allocation algorithm (detailed):
- Fast-path try: check per-core fast-bucket for microsegment with sufficient contiguous free space; if available, bump-allocate and update local LRU tick.
- Slow-path try: consult lane-local pool (lockless ring) for donor microsegments; if none, request from global allocator (centralized but rare). Global allocator tries to satisfy by stitching or taking from low-pressure lanes.
- Fallback: if global allocator cannot find free memory, trigger eviction sampler (policy above) and mark several microsegments as candidate for immediate reclaim; return allocation failure if still insufficient (caller backpressure).

Eviction selection & fairness:
- Sampling-based victim selection minimizes scan overhead and smooths fairness across lanes of different sizes.
- To prevent starving small tenants, maintain a minimum reserved fraction per tenant class. Operator-configurable SLOs: min-reserve-per-tenant, max-lane-pressure, global-eviction-aggressiveness.

Fragmentation control: the reshuffle algorithm (novelty):
- ISR uses a two-tier reshuffle: soft reshuffle (cheap, per-allocate/evict triggered) and hard reshuffle (budgeted background).
- Soft reshuffle: when an allocation fails inside a microsegment but the microsegment has reclaimable free holes from recent evictions (tombstones younger than a threshold), the allocator attempts an in-place micro-move: relocate a small set of entries within the same microsegment to make a contiguous hole for the allocation. This is cheap and keeps locality.
- Hard reshuffle: the worker picks a microsegment with free fraction > X and live occupancy < Y and performs relocation into a target microsegment, updating compact pointers and metadata atomically. The moving is cooperative and respects a per-worker CPU time cap.
- Stitcher uses heuristics to prefer coalescing adjacent free microsegments only if post-coalesce the resulting run length exceeds the requester size distribution 95th percentile. This prevents wasteful consolidation of tiny free runs.

Interaction with kernels and scheduling:
- Kernel: ISR keeps all critical fast-path ops lockless; the only kernel interactions are page pinning/unpinning and when resizing underlying memory pools. We avoid frequent madvise/mmap churn by reusing pages across microsegments and relying on stitcher to do large decommits.
- Scheduling: reshuffle workers are SCHED_BATCH-like with cgroup/rt-awareness; they yield aggressively on I/O or when tail latency signals spike. The runtime exposes a heartbeat-signal to the SRE stack so reshuffle can be throttled during peak SLO pressure.

Observability & telemetry:
- Key metrics: microsegment_free_fraction_histogram, per-lane_pressure, reshuffle_cycles_consumed, soft_reshuffle_success_rate, hard_compaction_latency_p50/p95/p99, stitcher_coalesce_rate, tombstone_resurrect_rate.
- Traces: record per-allocation path (fast/slow/fallback), victim_sampling_batch_id, and reshuffle task id. Sampling rate ~1:1000 for production.

Operational knobs and defaults:
- defaults: microsegment_size=16KB, lane_soft_quota=0.7*tenant_committed_bytes, soft-reshuffle-age=5s, hard-reshuffle-threshold_free=0.4, per-worker_time_budget_ms=5.
- Operators can tune: min-reserve-per-tenant, stitcher_aggressiveness, global-eviction-aggressiveness.

Rollout & experiments:
1) Canary on synthetic tenant with mixed seq-lens (A/B): compare memory-efficiency, p99 allocation latency, and tail compaction CPU.
2) Gradual ramp by tenant size: start with small tenants under low global pressure; monitor tombstone_resurrect_rate and reshuffle_cycles_consumed.
3) Stress test: bursty hot-prefix replay to validate tombstone TTL / resurrect behavior.

Bench plan (quick):
- Microbench: allocate/free traces sampled from production (3 tenants), run ISR vs baseline slabless and slab allocator variants. Measure: memory utilization, p50/p95/p99 alloc latency, background CPU overhead.
- System bench: run on 8-gpu pod with 64 tenants, simulate hot spikes. Measure tail latency under reshuffle throttle.

Open questions / risks:
- Metadata pressure: per-microsegment header size increases metadata working set—need to ensure header cacheability across NUMA nodes.
- Correctness of cooperative moves: must ensure atomicity guarantees for concurrent readers/writers—design sketch uses versioned headers and a small compare-and-swap window; requires thorough formalization.
- Garbage amplification under pathological access patterns (very interleaved small writes) — mitigate by adding microsegment eviction boost for such patterns.

Appendix: prototype milestones:
- Week 0-2: implement per-core fast-bucket and microsegment headers + simple bump allocator.
- Week 3-5: implement lane accounting, sampling eviction, tombstone path.
- Week 6-8: implement soft reshuffle in-place moves and lightweight stitcher.
- Week 9-12: implement hard reshuffle, metrics, and canary tests.

Notes-to-self / followups:
- Cross-ref with storage team's recently updated page layout (confluence:/pages/ISR-layout).
- Sync with sched team to expose reshuffle heartbeat hook and cgroup flags.
- Draft a short spec for the atomic relocation protocol for reviews.
